analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with tax deductions, expanded health savings accounts, and high-risk pools.
analysis.headline: This full repeal-and-replace bill drew 133 Republican cosponsors but never received a committee vote or floor action before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have erased the Affordable Care Act entirely, effective as if it had never passed, and replaced it with a conservative alternative: a large income tax deduction for people who buy their own health insurance, much-expanded health savings accounts, federally funded high-risk pools for people with preexisting conditions, the right to buy insurance across state lines, and caps on medical malpractice awards. Its supporters framed it as patient-centered reform; its structural effect was to end the ACA's subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and consumer protections while cutting taxes that fall on insurers, drug makers, and high-income households.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income taxpayers who buy their own coverage gain the most from the new deduction, which is worth more per dollar to people in higher tax brackets and is limited to earned income. Insurers, brand-name drug makers, device makers, and physicians gain from repeal of ACA taxes and rules. Healthy people in the individual market gain from lighter regulation and cross-state plan shopping. People with preexisting conditions get access to high-risk pools, though typically at higher premiums than the ACA's guaranteed coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a standard deduction for health insurance costs of $7,500 for an individual and $20,000 for a family, available whether or not the taxpayer itemizes and excluded from payroll taxes [S2][S3].

Greatly expands health savings accounts: higher contribution limits, spousal catch-up contributions, bankruptcy protection equal to retirement accounts, rollover of flexible spending account balances, and a $3,000-per-year deduction for child health savings accounts [S2][S3].
Authorizes $2.5 billion a year for fiscal years 2015 through 2023, plus startup grants of up to $5 million per state, for state high-risk pools covering people with preexisting conditions [S2][S3].
Applies federal antitrust laws to the business of health insurance, overriding the McCarran-Ferguson exemption, and makes Medicare claims and payment data public [S2][S3].
Caps noneconomic damages in health care lawsuits at $250,000, limits punitive damages, and preempts state malpractice law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Low- and moderate-income people lose the ACA's refundable tax credits and Medicaid expansion, which reach households too poor to benefit from a deduction. People with preexisting conditions lose guaranteed-issue protection in the individual market and are directed to risk pools with higher premiums. Injured patients face a $250,000 cap on malpractice compensation. The repeal also strips out the ACA's dedicated taxes on insurers, drug makers, devices, and high earners, shifting the cost of those lost revenues to future taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The replacement tax deduction is limited to earned income and is worth the most to taxpayers in higher brackets, while the ACA credits it replaces are refundable and aimed at lower- and middle-income households — so the swap tilts the benefit up the income scale [S2][S3].

The bill eliminates certain guaranteed-availability requirements in the individual market and relies on high-risk pools for people with preexisting conditions, funded at $2.5 billion a year, which is a thinner safety net than the ACA's open-market guarantee [S2][S3].

Insurers could sell plans across state lines under the rules of the state they choose; the bill's own required disclosure warns buyers that the policy 'is not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes' of their home state [S3].

Group plans could vary premiums and cost-sharing by up to 50 percent of the benefit's value based on participation in wellness programs, raising costs for workers who cannot meet the program's standards [S2][S3].
The $250,000 cap on noneconomic malpractice damages, preempting state law, would reduce compensation for patients seriously injured by medical error [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A few provisions are genuinely consumer-friendly — antitrust coverage for insurers, public Medicare payment data, and state price-transparency portals. But the bill's core is a full repeal of the ACA's coverage expansion, and its replacement channels the largest new benefits through the tax code, where deductions favor households with substantial income. An honest reading is that the trade would move money and coverage protections away from lower-income and sicker people toward insurers, drug makers, device makers, and higher earners, while offering high-risk pools of uncertain adequacy in exchange.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee from the day it was introduced until Congress ended — referred to eight committees and six subcommittees, with no markup or floor vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. David Roe (R-TN) introduced the bill on September 18, 2013, joined by 24 original cosponsors including Steve Scalise, Marsha Blackburn, Tom Price, and Mick Mulvaney [S1][S3].

It was referred the same day to eight House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Appropriations, and Rules — and over the following months to subcommittees on Health, Health/Employment/Labor/Pensions, the Constitution and Civil Justice, and Regulatory Reform and Antitrust [S1][S5].
All 133 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on [S4].
No committee ever reported the bill and the House never voted on it; it died on January 3, 2015, when the 113th Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: the ACA's tax credits, Medicaid expansion, guaranteed-issue protections, and taxes on insurers and high earners all stayed in force, so the people covered by them are better off than they would have been under this bill. The bill's intended beneficiaries — insurers freed of ACA taxes and rules, drug and device makers, and high-income households — gained nothing.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of a majority of House Republicans.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or floor vote on the bill despite its 133 Republican cosponsors, letting it die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — 133 Republican cosponsors, zero Democrats — and no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: Repeal ends the ACA's health insurer fee and medical loss ratio rules, removes guaranteed-availability requirements in the individual market, and lets insurers sell policies across state lines under their home state's lighter rules — the bill's own required notice tells buyers the policy may not be subject to all of their state's consumer protection laws. The antitrust and transparency provisions impose modest new discipline in return.

Full repeal restores the pre-ACA tax treatment of high earners, including the Medicare taxes on wages and investment income that helped fund the coverage expansion. The replacement health insurance deduction is also worth more per dollar to taxpayers in higher brackets.

Repeal of the ACA restores the rules in effect before the law, including the end of the mandated 50 percent discount brand-name manufacturers provided on drugs for seniors in the Medicare coverage gap.
Repeal eliminates the ACA's 2.3 percent excise tax on medical devices, a revenue source that helped pay for the law's coverage expansion.

The bill caps noneconomic damages at $250,000, limits punitive damages, and preempts state malpractice law, lowering liability exposure for doctors and their insurers while reducing compensation available to injured patients.

Repealing the Medicaid expansion and subsidies would leave hospitals and providers with more uninsured and uncompensated patients — the industry's financial interest and the public's interest in coverage run in the same direction here.
